related_questions.question: What is the ICD-10 code for elevated cholesterol levels?

text_blocks.snippet: The ICD-10-CM code for elevated cholesterol levels, specifically pure hypercholesterolemia (unspecified), is E78.00. This code is used to document and bill for cases where cholesterol levels are elevated without a specified underlying cause or type.

list.snippet: E78.00: This code specifically refers to "Pure hypercholesterolemia, unspecified".
Hypercholesterolemia: This term indicates high levels of cholesterol in the blood.
Pure: This implies that the elevated cholesterol is not due to a specific underlying condition, like diabetes or certain medications.
Unspecified: If the exact cause of the hypercholesterolemia is not clear, this code is used.

text_blocks.snippet: If the elevated cholesterol is linked to a specific condition, like type 2 diabetes, the code would be different. For example, if someone with type 2 diabetes also has elevated cholesterol, the code might be E78.5 (Hyperlipidemia, unspecified).
Therefore, when reporting elevated cholesterol levels in medical documentation and billing, the appropriate ICD-10-CM code is E78.00 unless a specific cause is identified.

related_questions.question: What is the ICD-10 code for R79 9?

text_blocks.snippet: ICD-10 code R79.9 refers to abnormal findings of blood chemistry, unspecified. This code is used when blood test results indicate an irregularity, but the specific abnormality isn't identified or categorized elsewhere in the ICD-10-CM system. It essentially serves as a placeholder when further investigation is needed to determine the exact nature of the blood chemistry issue.
snippet_highlighted_words: abnormal findings of blood chemistry, unspecified

list.title: R79:
list.snippet: This code range (R70-R79) in ICD-10-CM covers "Abnormal findings on examination of blood, without diagnosis".

list.title: R79.9:
list.snippet: Specifically, R79.9 is used for an unspecified abnormal blood chemistry finding. This means that while the blood test shows something is off, it doesn't fall into a more specific category like abnormal mineral levels (R79.0) or abnormal coagulation profiles (R79.1).

list.title: Unspecified:
list.snippet: The "unspecified" nature of R79.9 means that the exact nature of the abnormality isn't known or documented, and further testing or evaluation may be necessary.

related_questions.question: Is high cholesterol the same as hyperlipidemia?

text_blocks.snippet: Yes, high cholesterol is often used as a synonym for hyperlipidemia. Hyperlipidemia is the medical term for having high levels of fats, including cholesterol and triglycerides, in the blood. So, while "high cholesterol" is a more common way to refer to the condition, "hyperlipidemia" is the more formal and accurate clinical term.
